title: Generics and Wildcards
summary: Generics are invariant, wildcards recover controlled variance. Master PECS, erasure, and when to use a type parameter vs a wildcard.

Understanding Java Generics and Wildcards | by Youssef Hassan
When to use wildcards in Java Generics? - Stack Overflow

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **`List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`.** Generics are invariant by default. Wildcards are the *only* controlled way to get covariance and contravariance back. Memorise this: **`? extends T` gives you values out, `? super T` lets you push values in.** Everything else is commentary.

Generics are compile-time-checked parametric polymorphism. You parameterise a class, interface, or method with a type like `Box<T>` or `<T> T max(Collection<T> c)`, the compiler proves every put and get is consistent, then it erases `T` to `Object` or its bound. At runtime there is exactly one `ArrayList` class. That is the whole bargain: you get static safety with zero runtime representation, and you pay with erasure, invariant subtyping, and miserable error messages. A `List<Integer>` and a `List<String>` are the same class at runtime but incompatible types at compile time, deliberately.

Wildcards are anonymous type arguments for when you do not need a name. `?` means *some specific but unknown type*. `? extends Number` means *some unknown subtype of `Number`*. `? super Integer` means *some unknown supertype of `Integer`*. They do not add capability to the language — anything you can do with a wildcard you can do with a named type parameter. They subtract needless naming. Use a wildcard when the type is used only for flexible subtyping at one call site. Use a named `T` when two positions in a signature must refer to the *same* type. That distinction is the entire interview.
The mechanism: invariance, erasure, and capture

blocks.title: Why invariance forces wildcards
blocks.caption: Integer is a Number, but List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. Wildcards create a bounded family that both can belong to.
blocks.code:
graph TD
  Int[Integer] --> Num[Number]
  Dbl[Double] --> Num
  LInt[List Integer] --> LExt[List extends Number]
  LDbl[List Double] --> LExt
  LNum[List Number] --> LExt
  LInt -.no.-> LNum
  LDbl -.no.-> LNum

blocks.text: Java arrays are covariant and unsound: you can assign an `Integer[]` to a `Number[]`, then get an `ArrayStoreException` at runtime when you store a `Double`. Generics fixed that mistake by making `List<Integer>` and `List<Number>` unrelated types. Nothing flows between them without a wildcard. `List<? extends Number>` is not a supertype in the naive sense — it is a family of types, and the compiler treats the `?` as a fresh capture variable per use. That is why you can read a `Number` out of it but cannot safely put an `Integer` in: the compiler does not know which member of the family you actually have. `List<Integer>` could be hiding behind that reference, and a `Double` write would corrupt it. The trade-off is explicit: **safety demands you give up either reads or writes, never both.** Erasure is the second half. Because `T` disappears at runtime, you cannot do `new T()`, `instanceof T`, or `new T[10]`. The compiler inserts casts and bridge methods to preserve the illusion, and that illusion leaks the moment you mix raw types, reflection, or varargs.

blocks.caption: Every wildcard buys flexibility by selling something else.
rows: `List<T>` exact match
Full read and write with precise type
Accepts only one concrete instantiation; `addAll` becomes useless
Precision vs reusability: exact types are correct but too narrow for APIs
`? extends T` producer
Accepts `List<Integer>`, `List<Double>` wherever `List<T>` is expected
Becomes effectively read-only; `add(null)` is all you can write
Covariance vs mutability: you trade write access for subtype acceptance
`? super T` consumer
Accepts `List<Number>`, `List<Object>` as a sink for `T` values
Reads degrade to `Object`; you lose return-type information
Contravariance vs readability: you trade read precision for write acceptance
Named `<T>` method
Can relate argument to argument and to return type, e.g. `<T> T pick(List<T>)`
Extra type variable, harder signature, inference can fail cryptically
Expressiveness vs complexity: name a type only when two positions must match
Unbounded `<?>`
Maximum acceptance: works for `containsAll`, `size`, `clear`
No reads beyond `Object`, no writes at all
Generality vs utility: use only when you touch structure, not elements

blocks.text: The working rule is PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — but understand *why* it holds. If a method only pulls values out of a collection to do work, that collection is a producer and should be `? extends T`, because you want the widest set of callers and you never need to write. If a method only pushes values in, it is a consumer and should be `? super T`, because you want the widest set of sinks and you never need a precise read. If it does both, you need an exact `T` or two coordinated type variables, and wildcards are the wrong tool. The opinionated part: most production generics code is over-wildcarded. A simple `<T>` signature that is slightly narrower beats a clever `? super ? extends` signature nobody can call without a cast. Choose the weakest wildcard that compiles your real call sites, not the most general one that type-checks in theory.
How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Generics fail at boundaries where compile-time information is gone: raw-type legacy code, reflection, deserialisation, and arrays. The compiler warns about unchecked casts, teams suppress the warning, and heap pollution follows — a `List<String>` reference pointing at memory that actually holds an `Integer`. Nothing explodes until far away, when a hidden compiler-inserted cast fires and you get a `ClassCastException` on a line with no visible cast. The second classic failure is `? extends` in a mutable API. Someone exposes `List<? extends Employee>` as a field or setter, then every downstream `add` stops compiling and engineers route around it with raw types or `Object` casts, destroying the safety the wildcard was meant to provide. The third is generic varargs like `<T> void of(T... items)` silently creating a `Object[]` that aliases a `String[]`, which corrupts on the next write.

items: `ClassCastException` with no cast in source: symptom of heap pollution from an unchecked cast, raw-type assignment, or deserialised `List` that lied about its element type. Look for `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` upstream.

`UnsupportedOperationException`-style compile wall: `add` rejected on a `? extends T` collection. Symptom that you used covariance where you needed invariance. Fix is to change the API to an exact `List<T>` or a `? super T` sink.

`ArrayStoreException` vs compile error confusion: arrays fail at runtime, generics fail at compile time. If you see code converting `List<T>` to `T[]` via `(T[]) new Object[n]`, expect a `ClassCastException` at the call site.
`incompatible types: List<Integer> cannot be converted to List<Number>` in a method that only reads: symptom of missing `? extends`. Fix the parameter, not the call site.
`capture of ?` errors when copying between two wildcards: symptom that you need a private generic helper to give the wildcard a name so read and write can be correlated.

blocks.title: Never suppress and walk away
blocks.text: Every `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` is a loan against a future `ClassCastException`. If you must write one, isolate it in a tiny verified factory method that defensively copies, and document the invariant the compiler cannot check. The trade-off is localised risk versus distributed corruption.

Read the two examples as a decision procedure. `copy` needs to accept a `List<Integer>` source into a `List<Number>` destination, so both parameters must be wildcarded in opposite directions, and the `<T>` exists only to tie the element read from `src` to the element written to `dst`. Without that bridge the compiler cannot prove the transfer is sound. `swap` and `pickFirst` need exact `List<T>` because they both read and write the same structure — any wildcard there either blocks the write or degrades the return type to `Object`. The `reverse` idiom is the professional move: expose `List<?>` because callers should be able to reverse any list, then immediately delegate to a private `<T>` helper that captures the wildcard so the body can call `get` and `set` with the same `T`. The trade-off you are managing is API generosity versus implementation precision, and the helper lets you have both.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Why does this not compile?
items.text: You will be shown `List<Number> ns = new ArrayList<Integer>()` or an `add` into a `List<? extends Number>`. Say *invariance* in the first sentence, then explain the corruption it prevents: if the assignment were allowed, `ns.add(3.5)` would put a `Double` into an `Integer` list. Interviewers fail candidates who recite PECS without stating the counter-example.

items.title: Design addAll / copy
items.text: You will be asked to type `void addAll` or `copy(dest, src)`. Write `Collection<? extends E>` for the source and `List<? super T>` for the destination without hesitation, then justify each with producer vs consumer. The follow-up is why not `<S extends T>`: answer that the extra name adds nothing when the type appears once.

items.title: Wildcard vs generic method
items.text: You will be asked when `<T> void take(List<T>)` differs from `void take(List<?>)` or `<T extends Animal> void take(List<T>)` versus `void take(List<? extends Animal>)`. Answer: they accept the same calls, but only the named `T` lets you relate the argument to another argument or the return type, or to write into the same list inside the body.

items.title: The capture question
items.text: You will be asked to implement `reverse(List<?>)` or `swap` on a wildcarded list and hit a capture error. The expected move is the private `<T>` helper. Naming this pattern — *capture helper* — signals senior-level familiarity.

items.title: The erasure question
items.text: You will be asked why you cannot do `new T()`, `instanceof T`, or overload `foo(List<String>)` and `foo(List<Integer>)`. Answer: one shared runtime class, casts inserted by the compiler, and overloads that collide after erasure. Offer the workarounds — `Class<T>` token, factory `Supplier<T>`, or distinct method names — and name their cost: an extra parameter or lost type information.

items: `List<Integer>` is a subtype of `List<Number>` — false, and the most common fail. Subtyping on the element does not lift to subtyping on the container. That is what `? extends` is for.
`? extends Number` means you can add any `Number` — backwards. You can add nothing (except `null`) because the list might be a `List<Integer>` in disguise. Extends is for reading.
`? super Integer` means you get `Integer`s out — backwards. You get `Object`s out, because the list might be a `List<Object>`. Super is for writing.
`<T>` is more powerful than `?` so always use `<T>` — wrong trade-off. A type variable you use once is noise that complicates inference. Wildcards express *intent*: no relationship to maintain.

`Generics exist at runtime` — false outside of narrow cases like `Class<T>` tokens or anonymous subclass tricks. Erasure means `List<String>.class` does not exist, and reflection cannot recover element types reliably.
`PECS` is a syntax rule — it is a consequence, not a rule. The real rule is: covariance forbids writes, contravariance degrades reads. PECS just tells you which sacrifice each use-site makes.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Use wildcards at flexible boundaries, exact types where identity matters.
rows: Method only reads from a collection parameter
`List<? extends T>`
Maximises callers; compiler enforces read-only discipline for free
Method only writes to a collection parameter
`List<? super T>`
Maximises sinks; you accept every list that can hold a `T`
Return type or field
Exact `List<T>`, never a wildcard
Wildcards in returns force every caller to deal with `?`; you push complexity outward
Type relates two params or param to return
Named `<T>`, e.g. `<T> T getOrDefault(List<T>, T)`
Only a name can assert *same* type in two places; wildcards cannot
Class declaration
Named `T`, e.g. `Box<T>`, `Cache<K,V>`
The type must be referenced across methods and stored in fields; `?` cannot be stored
Heterogeneous or truly unknown data
`<?>` plus a capture helper, or a `Class<T>` token
Unbounded wildcard for structure-only ops; token when you need runtime behaviour back

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence
blocks.text: Generics are invariant with erased implementations, so use `? extends T` when you only read, `? super T` when you only write, and a named `<T>` only when two positions must be the same type.
